summary: Defines the format of IPv6 global unicast addresses. It obsoletes RFC 2374 and makes the Top Level Aggregator and Next Level Aggregator structure that RFC described historic. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This memo changes how worldwide addresses are carved up. The old plan with fixed levels is retired, and a simpler layout takes its place.

questions: what happened to ipv6 tla nla
what is the ipv6 subnet id
how long is an ipv6 interface id
subtitle: How a worldwide IPv6 address splits into routing prefix, subnet ID and interface ID, after the TLA/NLA scheme was retired.

tldr.problem: RFC 2374 defined an IPv6 address allocation structure with Top Level Aggregator (TLA) and Next Level Aggregator (NLA) fields, which was no longer thought the best approach.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3587 makes RFC 2374 and the TLA/NLA structure historic and describes the general global unicast format: a global routing prefix, a subnet ID and a 64-bit interface ID.
tldr.outcome: Allocation is now governed by a coordinated policy of the Regional Internet Registries, and the old SLA field lives on as the subnet ID. RFC 2374 is obsoleted.

today: RFC 3587 is Informational and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. It obsoleted RFC 2374 and made the TLA/NLA structure historic.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 2374, "An IPv6 Aggregatable Global Unicast Address Format", defined an IPv6 allocation structure that includes the Top Level Aggregator (TLA) and Next Level Aggregator (NLA). RFC 3587 replaces RFC 2374 and makes both it and the TLA/NLA structure historic.
sections.eli5: An older plan for handing out worldwide addresses is being retired, and this memo says what comes next.

sections.title: Why TLA/NLA Was Made Historic
sections.content:
The TLA/NLA scheme has been replaced by a coordinated allocation policy defined by the Regional Internet Registries (RIRs). Part of the motivation is technical: there is concern that TLA/NLA is not the technically best approach at this stage of IPv6 deployment. The rest is that allocation relates to policy and to stewardship of the address space and routing table size, which the RIRs have managed for IPv4.

RFC 2374 defined addresses for Format Prefix 001 (2000::/3). Although only 2000::/3 is currently being delegated by the IANA, implementations should not assume it is special, because the IANA might later delegate other unassigned portions for global unicast.

The Subnet Local Aggregator (SLA) field remains in function but is renamed subnet ID in the addressing architecture document.
sections.eli5: Instead of one fixed plan, the groups that hand out addresses now set the rules. The room-number part of the address stays but gets a new name.

sections.title: The Address Format
sections.content:
A global unicast address has a global routing prefix of n bits, a subnet ID of m bits and an interface ID of 128-n-m bits. The prefix is assigned to a site (a cluster of subnets or links) and is designed to be structured hierarchically by the RIRs and ISPs. The subnet ID identifies a subnet within the site and is structured by site administrators.

The architecture also requires that all unicast addresses except those starting with binary 000 have 64-bit interface IDs in Modified EUI-64 format. The layout is then n bits of prefix, 64-n bits of subnet ID and 64 bits of interface ID.

Under 2000::/3, consistent with the recommendations in RFC 3177, the example layout is 3 bits (001), a 45-bit global routing prefix, a 16-bit subnet ID and a 64-bit interface ID.
sections.eli5: The first part says which site you are at, the middle says which network inside the site, and the last part says which device. For the example, the last part is 64 bits long.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says only that IPv6 addressing documents do not have any direct impact on Internet infrastructure security.
sections.eli5: Choosing how addresses are split up does not by itself make the Internet less safe.

fields.name: Subnet ID
fields.desc: Identifies a subnet within the site.
